title: To, At, In and Into: Movement and Arrival
summary: Use to for destinations, in and at after arrive for different kinds of destinations, and into for entering a space. Learn the no-preposition patterns with home and the usual boarding and leaving expressions for transport.
learningObjectives: Use to after movement expressions and after visit-related expressions such as a trip to and welcome to.
Distinguish get to from arrive in for towns or countries and arrive at for buildings or events.
Use go home, get home and arrive home without to, in or at.
Describe entering a room or car with into and distinguish it from position in and transport expressions such as get on and get off.

explanation.heading: To marks a destination
explanation.body: After go, come, travel, drive, return and similar movement verbs, to usually identifies the destination. It is also used after expressions such as a trip to, a visit to, welcome to and on the way to. To marks movement towards a location, while in or at can describe where someone already is.
explanation.example: We drove to the coast, but our friends stayed in the city.

explanation.heading: Been to for places and experiences
explanation.body: Use have been to when you mean that someone has visited a place or attended an event, without claiming they are there now. This differs from have gone to, which often indicates that the person has left for that destination. The focus here is on the correct preposition after been.
explanation.example: I have been to the planetarium twice this year.

explanation.heading: Get to, arrive in and arrive at
explanation.body: With a destination, say get to the station or get to a town. After arrive, do not use to. Use arrive in with a city, town or country; use arrive at with buildings, destinations treated as points, and events. For example, arrive in Lisbon but arrive at the hotel. Use the relevant context to identify whether the place is a city or a venue.
explanation.example: They arrived in Valencia before midday and arrived at their apartment an hour later.

explanation.heading: Home follows movement verbs directly
explanation.body: Home behaves differently from ordinary destinations. Say go home, come home, get home and arrive home, without a preposition before home. Similarly, say on my way home, not on my way to home. The phrase at home describes being at home; it is not needed after these movement verbs.
explanation.example: After the late rehearsal, we went straight home.

explanation.heading: Into for crossing a boundary
explanation.body: Into normally describes movement from outside to inside a room, building, container or vehicle. In usually describes location after movement has finished. With get, go and put, in can sometimes replace into: get in the car and get into the car are both natural. For clear contrasts, into makes the movement or entry explicit.
explanation.example: A gust of wind pushed the leaves into the kitchen.

explanation.heading: Boarding and leaving different vehicles
explanation.body: With a bus, train or plane, we usually say get on and get off. With a car or taxi, say get in or get into, and get out of. The choice depends on the kind of vehicle; both on and in can appear elsewhere in transport descriptions, but these are the normal boarding and leaving patterns.
explanation.example: I got off the tram, then got into a taxi outside the station.

comparisons.title: Movement toward a venue versus presence there

left.label: To: destination
left.example: We are going to the exhibition.
left.note: To points to where the group is heading.

right.label: At: location
right.example: We are at the exhibition now.
right.note: At identifies the event where the group currently is.

left.label: Arrive in: city/country
left.example: The team arrived in Oslo on Wednesday.

right.label: Arrive at: building/venue
right.example: The team arrived at the research centre.
right.note: At identifies a particular building or venue.

comparisons.title: Entering a space versus being inside

left.label: Into: movement across a boundary
left.example: The cat ran into the shed.
left.note: The cat crossed from outside to inside.

right.label: In: position inside
right.example: The cat is hiding in the shed.
right.note: In describes where the cat is now.

comparisons.title: Leaving a bus versus leaving a car

left.label: Get off: bus or train
left.example: The tourists got off the bus.
left.note: Off is the usual particle for leaving a bus.

right.label: Get out of: car or taxi
right.example: The tourists got out of the taxi.
right.note: Out of is the normal expression for leaving a taxi.

examples.sentence: Welcome to our new community centre.
examples.note: Welcome to is the established expression introducing a place.

examples.sentence: We got to the stadium just before the gates opened.
examples.note: Get to can describe reaching a specific venue.

examples.sentence: The visitors arrived in Kyoto on Tuesday morning.
examples.note: A named city takes in after arrive.

examples.sentence: They arrived at the theatre in time for the performance.
examples.note: A building or venue normally takes at after arrive.

examples.sentence: I came home early to finish an assignment.
examples.note: Come home has no preposition before home.

examples.sentence: A bird flew into the garage through an open window.
examples.note: Into describes the bird crossing into the building.

examples.sentence: Please get off the bus at the next stop.
examples.note: Off is used for leaving a bus.

examples.sentence: The driver got out of the car to check the tyre.
examples.note: Out of describes leaving the inside of a car.

commonMistakes.why: Use arrive in with a city; arrive to is not the standard pattern.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I got to home just after midnight.
commonMistakes.correct: I got home just after midnight.
commonMistakes.why: Get home takes no preposition before home.
The established greeting is welcome to a place.

commonMistakes.incorrect: She got off the taxi outside the station.
commonMistakes.correct: She got out of the taxi outside the station.
commonMistakes.why: The normal expression for leaving a taxi is get out of, not get off.

studyTips: Group verbs by pattern: go to / return to / get to, arrive in a city, arrive at a venue, and get home with no preposition.
Draw an arrow from outside a room to inside it: describe the movement with into and the final position with in.
Practise a short journey aloud using four stages: get on the bus, get off the bus, get into a taxi, get out of the taxi.

exercises.prompt: We arrived ___ Edinburgh early in the morning and explored the old town.
exercises.feedback: Use arrive in with a city such as Edinburgh.

exercises.prompt: The guests are travelling ___ the conference venue by coach.
exercises.feedback: Travel to marks the destination of the journey.

exercises.prompt: When the meeting finished, everyone went ___ without waiting for another bus.
exercises.feedback: Go home takes no preposition; home follows went directly.

exercises.prompt: A small bird flew ___ the living room through an open window.
exercises.feedback: Into shows movement from outside to the inside of the room.

exercises.prompt: The team arrived ___ before the seminar started. (the university building; write the preposition and place)
acceptedAnswers: at the university building
exercises.feedback: A particular building takes at after arrive.

exercises.prompt: The visitors travelled ___ for a weekend exhibition. (Madrid; write the preposition and city)
acceptedAnswers: to Madrid
exercises.feedback: Travel to identifies Madrid as the destination.

exercises.prompt: After the long drive, Mia finally got ___ at eleven. (destination: her own home; write only the destination word)
acceptedAnswers: home
exercises.feedback: Get home uses home without a preposition.

exercises.prompt: The dog ran ___ through the open gate. (the garden; focus on crossing into it; write the preposition and place)
acceptedAnswers: into the garden
exercises.feedback: Into describes the dog entering the garden through the gate.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the incorrect location preposition in this sentence: The students arrived to Vienna on Monday afternoon.
acceptedAnswers: The students arrived in Vienna on Monday afternoon.
exercises.feedback: A city takes in after arrive, not to.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the unnecessary preposition before home in this sentence: After the concert, we went to home by bicycle.
acceptedAnswers: After the concert, we went home by bicycle.
exercises.feedback: Go home does not take to; remove that preposition.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the incorrect location preposition in this sentence: Welcome in the new exhibition centre!
acceptedAnswers: Welcome to the new exhibition centre!
exercises.feedback: The greeting takes welcome to, not welcome in.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the incorrect transport expression in this sentence: We got off the taxi outside the office.
acceptedAnswers: We got out of the taxi outside the office.
exercises.feedback: Passengers normally get out of a taxi, whereas they get off a bus or train.

speakingExercises.prompt: Give a complete sentence using these facts: the tourists / travel / to the museum / yesterday. Use the past simple and begin with “The tourists”.
acceptedAnswers: The tourists travelled to the museum yesterday.
speakingExercises.feedback: Travel to identifies the tourists’ destination.

speakingExercises.prompt: The visitors have reached Berlin. Say one sentence using “arrived in Berlin” and starting with “The visitors”. Use the past simple.
acceptedAnswers: The visitors arrived in Berlin.
speakingExercises.feedback: Arrive in takes a city or country.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the preposition and say the whole sentence: “We arrived to the library at nine.”
acceptedAnswers: We arrived at the library at nine.
speakingExercises.feedback: Arrive at takes a specific building; arrive to is not the standard construction.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your friend asks when you reached your own home. Fact: I / get home / at eight. Reply in one sentence in the past simple.
acceptedAnswers: I got home at eight.
speakingExercises.feedback: Got home has no preposition between got and home.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make one sentence: a child / walk / into the classroom / quietly. Use the past simple and start with “A child”.
acceptedAnswers: A child walked into the classroom quietly.
speakingExercises.feedback: Into describes crossing the classroom doorway.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say you have visited Scotland twice. Start with “I have” and use the exact expression “been to Scotland twice”.
acceptedAnswers: I have been to Scotland twice.
I've been to Scotland twice.
speakingExercises.feedback: Have been to describes previous visits without implying you are there now.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences. First: we / get on the train / at noon. Second: we / get off the train / at three. Use the past simple and begin each sentence with “We”.
acceptedAnswers: We got on the train at noon. We got off the train at three.
speakingExercises.feedback: Use got on to board a train and got off to leave it.

speakingExercises.prompt: A passenger wants to leave a taxi at the next stop. Give one imperative sentence beginning with “Get”, using “out of the taxi”, and ending with “at the next stop”.
acceptedAnswers: Get out of the taxi at the next stop.
speakingExercises.feedback: Get out of is the normal expression for leaving a taxi.

listeningExercises.audioText: We arrived in Zagreb yesterday evening, but it was nearly midnight when we reached our hotel.
choices: The travellers arrived in the city.
listeningExercises.feedback: They arrived in Zagreb in the evening and reached the hotel later.

listeningExercises.audioText: I went to the market to buy fresh vegetables. My sister stayed at home to finish her project.
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker went to the market; the sister remained at home.

listeningExercises.audioText: The guests arrived at the theatre twenty minutes before the show began.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four-word location phrase immediately after “arrived”.
acceptedAnswers: at the theatre
listeningExercises.feedback: Arrive at identifies a specific venue or building.

listeningExercises.audioText: A fox ran into the garden through a hole in the fence, then hid under the bench.
listeningExercises.prompt: Where did the fox move first?
listeningExercises.feedback: The fox crossed the fence boundary and entered the garden.

listeningExercises.audioText: We missed the morning bus, so we travelled by train and got off at the central station.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which vehicle did the travellers leave at the station?
listeningExercises.feedback: They missed the bus, travelled by train and then got off the train.

listeningExercises.audioText: I have been to Canada twice, but my cousin has lived there since childhood.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker say about their own experience?
choices: They have lived in Canada since childhood.
listeningExercises.feedback: Have been to Canada twice describes visits, not permanent residence.

listeningExercises.audioText: After the rehearsal, Jamie went home without stopping for dinner.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word movement expression immediately after “Jamie”.
acceptedAnswers: went home
listeningExercises.feedback: Went home takes no preposition before home.

listeningExercises.audioText: The passengers got off the bus beside the library.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word transport expression immediately after “passengers”.
acceptedAnswers: got off the bus
listeningExercises.feedback: Get off the bus describes leaving that vehicle.
